questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The defining factor in choosing my study destination (Vancouver, Canada) was a mix between academic opportunities and the possibility to explore a beautiful country and nature. I have definitely not been disappointed.  British Columbia has offered some of the most amazing cultural and natural experiences I have ever had. From surfing on Vancouver Island, hiking in the mountains around Vancouver and Banff/Jasper to skiing in Whistler and Big White, I have had the experience of a lifetime. Moreover, the University of British Columbia offers a great academic program from an international perspective. I have made many new good friends both from Denmark and from around the world.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Fantastic experience. I would recommend everyone to attend UBC. The nature is amazing and the academic level is reasonable ie you still have time to do a lot other than just study.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy - GoGlobal, UBC and UCPH provide you with the necessary information. However, I would recommend researching information on insurance etc. on your own time. I was only covered by iMED which is mandatory as a student at UBC. This is sufficient if you only stay within British Columbia. However, I was very unsure if this was the case and if it was necessary to have insurance besides iMED. This can be necessary if you want to go skiing after the end of the semester, and it is often mandatory to make a private insurance agreement BEFORE departing for Canada. I would recommend you to make such an agreement before departing for Canada - but only with covering after the end of the iMED period. Alternatively, I think it is possible to extend iMED for the period in question.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received some general information via e-mail. It is pretty straightforward. There is also a lot of information on the webpage of UBC.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Make use of the many different possibilities offered by UBC. For instance, you can join a team - football, volleyball etc. Moreover, there are free recreational facilities, for instance for swimming, basketball, badminton etc.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I was one of the only exchange students offered on campus housing due to Covid. I lived at Fairview Crescent which was great. There is a great environment, and it is pretty cozy. However, the beds are pretty terrible. Expect to buy all every-day interior yourself (plates, cooking-gear). Beds, sofas etc. are provided by the University.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There are meal plans available. Did not use them tho.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is EXPENSIVE to cook yourself. I ate out a lot due to a small price-difference between eating out compared to cooking yourself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The beds were really terrible and we had some problems with water running from the ceiling. Otherwise, it worked out fine and it is really close to campus. Moreover, there are a lot of possibilities for takeaway+groceries around the corner.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You make an ordered list of priorities for courses. Be prepared not to get your first priorities. I am a graduate student, however, I could only attend undergraduate courses. Therefore, the academic level was significantly lower than what I was used to from UCPH. Upon arrival, I am told it is possible to attend graduate-level courses if you contact the individual professors. 

The only difficult thing about the process is to get course descriptions in order to get merit at UCPH. These are not publicly available. You have to contact the individual professors - and not all of them respond. However, you can be lucky that UCPH has already accepted the course as available for merit transfer. Therefore, I would recommend writing to UCPH first with your preferred courses and ask if UCPH has already accepted some of the courses, befrore you contact the professors at UBC.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: E-mails from UBC explain the process very carefully.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Pretty unsuccessful - got a mix of the classes I wanted and didn't want. However, I ended up dropping some of my unwanted courses at the end of the registration period. For instance, I got a course in Political Economics which I was really happy about.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Contact UCPH with a list of your preferred courses and ask if they are already accepted for transferring credits. The professors at UBC don't always send you a course description upon request.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In an international perspective, UBC is very good. However, the academic level was too low for me. I am a graduate student and only got undergraduate courses. Moreover, be prepared that assignments and participation counts towards the final grade.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The course level was not very high. However, there is a big gap in difficulty between 300 and 400 courses. 400 courses are pretty demanding. For instance, International Trade (ECON455) and Economics of Renewable resources (ECON472) were pretty difficult and interesting. However, be prepared that the biggest part of your work should be focused on the assignments and the midterms. The final exam counts for around 25-40% of your final grade. By that point, if you have done well on the assignments/midterms/term paper you could already have passed the class before the final exam. This could be important seeing that grades are only transferred as passed/not passed to UCPH with passed being >50%. Moreover, for many students at UBC, there is a "finals week" where all your exams are placed. Therefore, there are lower expectations for students at the final exam. To this end, it should be noted that difficult exams are "curved", such that you receive additional points if the overall score of the class is low. This is different from UCPH. I personally think that UBC is more interested in keeping a high score for their students, seeing that they depend on tuition.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I had a lot of courses where attendance was graded. This was pretty weird - I prefer the teaching style at UCPH. However, I liked the way that assignments count towards the final grade. This creates an incentive to follow the course closely - and takes pressure off the final exam.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Economics of Renewable Ressources (Econ 472)
International Trade (Econ 455) 
Economics of Technological Change (Econ 339)
International Political Economy (Poli 366)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: International Trade (Econ 455) and Economics of Renewable Ressources (Econ 472). Both are demanding but interesting. I cannot recommend Econ 339. The professor had a very irritating teaching style with an overemphasis on being pedagogical.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food is expensive. I also had a pretty large budget, so I prioritized eating out several times a week. Moreover, every chance I got, we traveled out of Vancouver. This entails several extra costs for transportation, food and gear (especially skiing!).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is expensive. Moreover, if you wan't to experience the country I would recommend buying a car. I bought one with two friends for +-20000 in total (4000 dollars). If your car does not break (as ours did :-)) then the resell value should be pretty close to the original price of the car.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Simply Fantastic!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I joined a soccer team - an invaluable experience. Made a lot of new great friends.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a team of some sort. There are a lot of possibilites.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Hike in the mountains, visit Banff/Jasper, go to Whistler, surf in Tofino, visit Victoria. We also made a road trip to California.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Vancouver is pretty European in mindset. There are surprisingly many Asians. I would guess that there are more Chinese students than native canadians.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs and link up with the other students from UCPH. We had a great group of 12 people from UCPH with whom I traveled a lot with.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not any

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendliness and respect. Be prepared to chat to people in grocery stores.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1) Go explore the crazy nature of Canada, 2) Buy a car, 3) Be extrovert - see if you can join some of the Whatsapp groups for exchange students.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Have a Canadian credit card if you want to stay at a hotel on Vancouver Island! Danish credit cards does not work. You can create a credit card at a bank such as RBC or CIBC.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The nature experiences. I have been on the greatest hikes, road trips, and skiing trips.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing school with all the opportunities outside school.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I would 1000% recommend UBC to anyone. Experience of a lifetime.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
